ISRO Prepares GSLV-F17 Rocket to Launch EOS-05 Earth Observation Satellite

30 Oct 2026, 09:28 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Science Desk · Source: news.abplive.com

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is scheduled to launch the EOS-05 advanced Earth observation satellite aboard the GSLV-F17 mission from Sriharikota. Operating from a geosynchronous orbit approximately 36,000 kilometres above Earth, the mission aims to provide continuous monitoring capabilities for both strategic and civilian applications.

Understanding the Geosynchronous Orbit Advantage

Most of India's Earth observation constellations, such as the Cartosat and RISAT series, function in low Earth orbit (LEO) at altitudes ranging from roughly 60 km to 2,000 km. Satellites in LEO circle the globe and provide periodic imagery of specific locations rather than continuous coverage.

In contrast, a geosynchronous orbit matches the Earth's rotation speed, allowing a satellite positioned 36,000 km above the surface to maintain a persistent view over a fixed region. Also designated as GISAT-1A, EOS-05 is designed to deliver frequent imagery of the Indian subcontinent, supporting applications that require sustained observation.

Capabilities and Applications

According to mission parameters, EOS-05 is equipped with two multispectral imaging instruments. One of these features a spatial resolution of 42 metres per pixel, noted as the highest-resolution camera placed in a geostationary orbit for India's space program.

The satellite's persistent-monitoring capacity is intended to aid in tracking rapidly developing events such as severe weather, fires, and ground changes, alongside providing strategic border surveillance capabilities.

Context of the GSLV-F17 Mission

This launch marks a renewed effort following the August 2021 failure of the GISAT-1 mission, where a technical malfunction in the cryogenic upper stage of the GSLV-F10 rocket prevented proper ignition. The upcoming GSLV-F17 flight also represents ISRO's return to the launchpad following an operational gap of approximately eight months.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers looking to verify official mission details can consult updates directly through the Indian Space Research Organisation or reference initial reports via outlets like ABP Live at https://news.abplive.com/science/isro-naughty-boy-gslv-set-for-liftoff-with-eos-05-off-what-will-it-do-explained-1865052.

  • Confirmed Facts: EOS-05 will operate at roughly 36,000 km altitude in geosynchronous orbit; it carries two multispectral imaging payloads including a 42-metre per pixel resolution instrument; it follows the 2021 GISAT-1 launch failure.
  • What Remains Unknown: Specific real-time operational milestones following the initial liftoff sequence and exact operational calibration timelines are subject to post-launch telemetry announcements by ISRO.
